name: CoolTone
lead: CoolTone is a magnetic muscle-stimulation device marketed for body contouring, and it is discussed in appearance circles as an add-on to fat-reduction treatments such as cryolipolysis ("fat freezing"), the technology behind CoolSculpting.[1][2] Magnetic muscle stimulation uses a changing magnetic field to make targeted muscles contract, with the aim of increasing tone.

Published evidence located for this entry is minimal. The only record found is a small registered clinical trial, started in 2022 with 15 participants, that compares CoolSculpting combined with CoolTone against CoolSculpting alone for the "banana roll" area beneath the buttocks.[1] Its status is listed as unknown and no results were found. Cryolipolysis itself has been studied more extensively, with a 2023 review of 18 studies reporting modest ultrasound-measured fat thickness reductions and low data quality.[2]

paras: CoolTone is described in a clinical trial registration as being used alongside CoolSculpting for the banana roll region, the fold of tissue under the buttock.[1] Cryolipolysis, the companion technology, uses controlled cooling to reduce localized subcutaneous fat; it was introduced in the United States in 2010 and its maker was acquired by Allergan in 2017.[2]

One registered trial (NCT05359614) compares CoolSculpting with CoolTone against CoolSculpting alone for the banana roll area in 15 participants. The trial began in March 2022, and its status is listed as unknown with no published results.[1] No other human studies of CoolTone were found for this article.

For the companion technology, a 2015 systematic review of 19 cryolipolysis studies reported skinfold reductions of 10.3% to 28.5%, and a 2023 review of 18 studies reported ultrasound-measured fat thickness reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm, with the authors describing the data quality as low.[2]

No safety data specific to CoolTone were found. For cryolipolysis, reported effects include redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, and paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which treated fat enlarges, has been reported in roughly 0.12% to 1.0% of cases depending on the study.[2]

timeline.event: A 15-person trial of CoolSculpting with CoolTone versus CoolSculpting alone begins.[1]

card.summary: A magnetic muscle-stimulation add-on to fat freezing, with almost no published evidence of its own.
card.note: Only one small registered trial found, with no results.

quick.overview:
CoolTone is a device that uses magnetic fields to make muscles contract, marketed for toning areas such as the lower buttock. It is discussed alongside fat-freezing treatments.

The only human study found is a 15-person registered trial, with no results available.
quick.mechanism: Magnetic muscle stimulation induces muscle contractions in the treated area; the intent is increased tone. No mechanistic study specific to CoolTone was found.
quick.risks: No CoolTone-specific safety data were found. The related fat-freezing procedure has reported side effects including redness, numbness, bruising and, rarely, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia.
